newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya unveils bourse plans for next three years.
newsitem.headline: Kenya unveils bourse plans for next three years.

text.p: Kenya's bourse regulators on Thursday unveiled ambitious development plans for the Nairobi Stock Exchange (NSE), including a possible review of restrictions on foreign investment this year.

Paul Melly, chief executive of Kenya's regulatory Capital Markets Authority (CMA), said rules limiting foreign investment in a listed company to 40 percent and individual foreign investment in such a firm to five percent would be reviewed.
"We will do it very soon. We may surprise you," Melly told a workshop in the capital. He later told Reuters that the review could come as early as this year.

In his vision for development to the year 2000, Melly saw the number of brokerage houses unchanged at 20, listed companies up to 75 from 60 with five public listings per year, doubled capitalisation and tripled volume of shares traded on the NSE.
"We don't think it is ambitious or unrealistic," he said.
Melly listed several other actions to develop the market:
-- Enhancing the trading mechanism at the bourse through adoption of an electronic trading system. He said a study on how this could be implemented would be undertaken before end-1997.

-- A central depository system to meet the pressing problem of clearing and registration of securities. He said project directors had been appointed and relevant legislation would be passed to parliament for approval.
-- Development of dealers as market participants at the bourse to facilitate improved liquidity. He said a framework for this would be finalised before the end of the year.

-- Encouraging the development of merchant banks as institutions to deal with securities issues, corporate finance and arranging for underwriting services. He said the CMA and the central bank would agree on how best to meet that need.
-- Development of a rating agency necessary for credit risk assessment, especially in issuing financial instruments such as corporate debts and general rating of companies.

Melly said there was a structural problem at the Nairobi Stock Exchange, where a majority of companies listed averaged only 20 percent of total capitalisation, with the remainder block shareholders and not available for trading.

In measures to raise the supply of securities, Melly said the CMA looked at new private sector listings through the capital markets and a review of the minimum public share issue for listing at the bourse from 20 percent to 25-30 percent.

He also spoke of addressing the issues of taxation that inhibit institutional investors such as insurance companies. Insurance firms have complained of taxes they perceive as either discriminatory or amounting to double taxation.

Melly said Kenya would encourage cross-border listing with Tanzania and Uganda, new financial instruments such as corporate and treasury bonds, asset-backed securities, commercial paper and strengthen CMA's regulatory role.
He said the CMA would implement simplified but comprehensive minimum standards for disclosure to ensure adequate disclosure of financial information by issuers of corporate securities.
The Nairobi bourse is capitalised at around $1.15 billion.
